issues.issue: The recital states that term loan lenders "shall provide" approximately US$530,000,000 and Project financing of US$713,000,000, while the operative "Total Commitment" definition fixes the commitment at US$250,000,000 and Section 2.20 makes any Accession Project Financing wholly discretionary. A court could be asked whether the recital creates an obligation the operative text does not.

"[A]ny material property or assets" sets no threshold, so the date on which the Borrower's additional-collateral obligations are triggered has no ascertainable boundary. The word "material" is undefined anywhere in Section 1.01.

The closing condition "on the same terms as the required by the Loans" is grammatically incomplete, leaving unclear what comparison of prepayment terms triggers inclusion of items (ii) and (iii) in the denominator. The whole pro rata fraction turns on that clause.

The definition closes each limb with "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Additional Obligations", defining the term by reference to itself. The circularity leaves the outer boundary of the secured Additional Obligations undetermined.

The definition ends with an open catch-all — "each other security agreement or other security instrument or document executed and delivered to the reasonable satisfaction of the Security Agent" — after a list of specific document types. Its reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain.

"Agents" is defined to include the Intercreditor Agent, but the "Intercreditor Agent" definition contemplates that no such agent may ever be appointed and the "Common Project Financing Facility" definition says an Intercreditor Agreement is only permissive. Whether "Agents" obligations bind a non-existent party is left open.

"Borrowing" is defined as "(a) a Term Loan or (b) an LC Exposure", equating a loan with an exposure amount rather than a credit extension. That mismatch makes provisions keyed to a "Borrowing" (minimum size, Borrowing Request, Interest Period) hard to apply to limb (b).

The phrase "commercial banks in the Hibbing, Minnesota, New York, New York, and Singapore are authorized or required by law to remain closed" is ungrammatical, and it is unclear whether closure in any one, or all, of the three centres suffices. The stray "the" and the missing conjunction leave the test unfixed.

Cash counts only if held at institutions "acceptable to the Lenders", a standard with no criteria and no reasonableness qualifier. Clause (c) also runs on with an unclosed parenthesis after "the Security Documents".

"Cash Available" and "Cash Sweep Cash Available" use the identical five components but only the latter carries the "without double counting" opener and the maintenance-capex deduction. Whether the DSCR and the Cash Sweep DSCR are meant to measure the same cash is left unresolved.

The definition adds "scheduled repayments of Loans to Project Lenders" to "corresponding scheduled repayments of any Supplier Financing", but the Recitals define "Project Lenders" to include the providers of supplier's credit. Read with that recital definition the supplier debt is counted twice.

The First Sweep Period mechanism operates "for each Sweep Date occurring in such period", but "Sweep Date" requires a full fiscal quarter within the period and "First Sweep Period" (nine months after a Scheduled Commercial Operations Date that may be as late as 30 June 2013, to 1 April 2014) may contain none. On those definitions limb (i) can be a dead letter.

The parenthetical "(a \"Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount\")" is placed on the DSCR result in excess of 1.15 rather than on the fifty percent payment figure, so the defined term labels the wrong quantity. Limb (i) places the parallel label on the payment amount, so the two limbs define "Sweep Amount" differently.

Sweep Amounts are to be paid out of the DSRA to the extent the Escrow Account is short, yet the DSRA must be maintained at the Required Amount under Section 5.15 and is topped up as cash collateral under Section 2.06(j). Which obligation prevails on a deficient Sweep Payment Date is not stated.

The period runs from nine months after the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date to 1 April 2014, but "Scheduled Commercial Operations Date" may be as late as 30 June 2013, which would make the First Sweep Period a single day (or none at all). That cannot be squared with the First Sweep Period limb of the Cash Sweep Mechanism.

"[E]ach full fiscal quarter during the applicable Sweep Period" is unclear as to whether the quarter must fall wholly inside the Sweep Period or merely end during it. The result decides whether any Sweep Date arises in the short First Sweep Period.

The definition makes the Sweep Payment Date one Business Day after the last day of the quarter "in which a Sweep Date occurs", which pushes payment a full quarter after the measurement quarter; the worked example is needed to make the text intelligible. Whether the example or the words govern is arguable.

A Change in Control is triggered at "more than 49%" of voting Equity Interests, a threshold below control, and the carve-out "other than by EGL or its Affiliates" is undefined as to indirect acquisitions. The mismatch with an ordinary majority test invites argument.

The date depends on the Engineering Consultant certifying that "commercial production has commenced", a term nowhere defined and with no output or duration benchmark. Both limbs must occur, so the certification controls a date on which sweep and covenant tests turn.

The definition requires certification by "the Lenders' Engineering Consultant", a term that appears nowhere in Section 1.01; the defined party is the "Engineering Consultant". Whether they are the same person is left to inference.

The facility is described as one in which the Lenders "become a party" and which "may be subject to an Intercreditor Agreement", leaving both the mechanism of accession and the intercreditor arrangement optional and unspecified. The pari passu promise has no defined machinery behind it.

"Control" turns on the "power to direct or cause the direction of the management or policies of a Person ... by contract or otherwise", a formulation whose outer edge ("or otherwise") is undefined. It drives the Affiliate definition and the affiliate-transaction restrictions.

"[O]ther assets that are due, or likely to be converted into cash, sold, exchanged, or expensed in the normal course of business, within one (1) year" makes the class turn on the vague predicate "likely". The boundary matters because the Security Agreement subordinates the Lenders' lien over Current Assets.

Limb (c) captures "all scheduled amortization repayments of any other Indebtedness" although limbs (a) and (b) are finance charges and lease principal, so "other" has no clear antecedent. What debt service is actually counted is therefore uncertain.

The term takes its meaning from "the Guarantee Agreement", singular, but the defined term is "Guarantee Agreements" and there are two (Exhibit E-1 for EGL and E-2 for the Parent). Which instrument supplies the release date is not stated.

After four named contracts the definition sweeps in "any other material contract entered into by the Borrower with respect to any engineering, procurement or construction services", with no threshold for materiality. The reach of the catch-all against the enumerated specifics is open.

The Borrower must deposit "all Cash and receivables arising out of any contracts of the Borrower with any Person or payments otherwise received by Borrower", a sweep with no carve-out and no stated boundary. Its width against the Borrower's working-capital needs is left to construction.

Amounts in the Escrow Account are said to be applied "in accordance with the Cash Sweep Mechanism", yet Section 2.05 directs all loan advances into the same Escrow Account for disbursement to the Borrower for its Borrowing Request purposes. The two uses of one account are not reconciled here.

The definition omits the operative verb — "'Existing Credit Agreement' the Credit Agreement dated September 22, 2010" — leaving a sentence fragment. The meaning is recoverable but the drafting slip is on the face of the text.

"Financial Closure" requires Total Commitments of US$530,000,000 and Supplier Financing "made available" of US$182,750,000, but says nothing about who must procure them or what "made available" requires. The trigger for the Tranche B facility therefore rests on an unallocated and unmeasured condition.

The definition can only be satisfied if Subsequent Project Lenders accede under Section 2.20, which is discretionary, yet the Recitals state that term loan lenders "shall provide" US$530,000,000 and Section 2.02(b) makes the Initial Lender's own Tranche B available only after Financial Closure. Read together the Borrower's access to committed money depends on an event no party is bound to bring about.

A long list of specific events closes with "or other similar acts beyond the reasonable control of the Borrower", a general catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is the classic ejusdem generis question. The 90-day/consultant qualifier adds a second undefined gate.

The definition extends to "related proceedings thereto that may be filed elsewhere in Federal or state court", an open-ended addition to a specifically identified action. Which future proceedings are "related" is left undetermined.

The list of hedging types closes with "or other derivative transaction of any kind or nature", an unbounded catch-all sitting against the named categories. Because Indebtedness includes all Hedging Agreement obligations, its width has real consequences.

Limb (f) sweeps in "any put options, shortfall undertakings, letters of comfort or any obligation undertaken by such Person in the nature of a payment obligation", a catch-all far wider than the specific debt categories preceding it. Whether ordinary contractual payment obligations become "Indebtedness" is genuinely arguable.

The Intercreditor Agreement is defined only as one "in form and substance satisfactory to the Borrower and the Required Lenders", with no terms fixed — an agreement to agree on the instrument that is to rank the secured parties. Nothing in the definition says what happens if satisfaction is withheld.

The term is defined as a "one-time request", while Section 2.07 is headed "Interest Elections" and speaks of an election operating for the initial and all subsequent Borrowings. Whether any later election is possible is unclear on the two texts together.

The definition refers to "the Borrowing of which such Loan is a part" although no Loan has been mentioned in the sentence, leaving the antecedent missing. The date on which interest falls due therefore has to be inferred.

The enumeration runs "(i) ... and (iii)" with no clause (ii), and the following proviso restarts at "(a), (b), (c)" although the definition already uses (a) and (b) as its main limbs. A clause appears to have dropped out of the operative mechanism for subsequent Borrowings.

Limb (b) opens "the sum of (i) ..." but never numbers a second element, running straight into "plus the aggregate amount of all LC Disbursements". The broken enumeration obscures what a single Lender's LC Exposure comprises.

The definition limits "Lender" to assignees that become "a Project Lender", a term the Recitals define to include providers of supplier's credit rather than only term lenders. The two definitions pull in different directions on who can be a Lender.

The closing words "on the same terms as the required by the Loans" are grammatically incomplete, so the condition on which items (ii) and (iii) enter the denominator cannot be applied as written. The Lender's entire prepayment share turns on that clause.

Unlike the parallel "Upstream Supplier Financing Creditor's Pro Rata Interest" and "Additional Indebtedness Holder's Pro Rata Interest" definitions, this one omits the "(and not an optional prepayment)" qualifier and cites Section 2.11(b) rather than 2.11(f). The three shares of one pro rata allocation are not drafted consistently.

The definition caps expiry at the earlier of 36 months from issuance or four years from the date of the Agreement (29 December 2014), yet clause (4) permits negotiation as late as 30 December 2014. The two internal deadlines cannot both be met.

Letters of Credit may be issued to 30 June 2013 and drawn long afterwards, but Section 2.06(e) converts every LC Disbursement into a Term Loan while Section 2.01 provides that undrawn Term Loan Commitments "lapse automatically" at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period on 30 September 2013. How a Term Loan arises after that lapse is unexplained.

The rate is taken from the Reuters "LIBOR01" screen, while the "Market Disruption Event" definition tests availability of the Reuters "LIBO01" screen rate. The two definitions identify the reference source differently.

After a closed list of named instruments the definition adds "any other document designated from time to time as a Loan Document by the Lenders or the Facility Agent", allowing one side unilaterally to expand the category. The scope of that catch-all against the enumerated documents is open to construction.

Limb (a) sweeps in "deferred payment guaranties, shortfall undertakings or payment undertakings or any nature whatsoever", a garbled catch-all (apparently for "of any nature") whose reach beyond the named categories is undefined. It sits directly against the specific instruments listed before it.

Each limb depends on what "Required Lenders determine", including limb (iii)'s cost of matching deposits and limb (iv)'s availability of deposits, with no objectivity or good-faith standard. The lenders' own determination decides whether the pricing basis disappears.

"Material adverse effect on ... the business, financial condition, operations or performance or properties of the Borrower since March 31, 2010" fixes neither a measure of materiality nor a coherent comparison date. Material adverse effect language of this kind is the standard subject of construction fights.

"[A]ll material approvals and consents by any Person" is bounded only by an "including, but not limited to" list, so the class of approvals whose absence breaches the conditions is indeterminate. "Material" is not defined.

The arithmetic is garbled — "the sum of (A) ... minus, (B) ... and (C) minus mark-to-market amounts" — so it is unclear whether (C) is added or subtracted, and the US$25,000,000 test's referent is equally unclear. A financial covenant computed on this formula cannot be applied with confidence.

The tax deduction refers to "any such event in respect of any Foreign Subsidiary", but "Foreign Subsidiary" is undefined and the "Subsidiary" definition records that the Borrower has none. The limb has no operative referent in this instrument.

Both limbs close "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Obligations", so the definition of Obligations is expressed by reference to itself. The circularity leaves the secured perimeter to be worked out by construction.

"Obligor" means "any of the Borrowers or any Guarantor", using a plural that does not exist: "Borrower" is defined as the single entity Essar Steel Minnesota LLC. The mismatch is a drafting slip on the face of the definition.

Several limbs turn on undefined materiality tests — Liens that "secure amounts that are not material to the value of the properties to which such Liens attach" and encumbrances that do not "materially adversely affect the value" — and the closing proviso reads "any Lien securing Indebtedness on Attributable Debt". The permitted-lien perimeter is not fixed by the words.

Limb (e) permits repurchase agreements "with a maturity not less than one (1) year thereafter", the opposite of the short-maturity limit applied to every other permitted investment. On its face the words admit the least liquid instruments in a liquidity definition.

Three stacked provisos alternately require and dispense with the Required Lenders' prior written consent for de-bottlenecking and similar modifications, so whether consent is needed depends on how the exceptions interact. The opening words already require consent, which the second proviso then removes in defined circumstances.

The sentence "includes any Permitted Project Change subject to the receipt of approval, if any, required in the definition of Permitted Project Change has been approved as set forth in the definition of that term" is ungrammatical and doubles back on itself. Whether an unapproved change falls within the Project cannot be read off the words.

The definition carves out contracts below a US$4,000,000 "Contract Threshold" and those listed on Schedule 1.01E, then requires "commercially reasonable efforts" to obtain consents even for the excluded ones, and then redefines the term again for Sections 6.09 and 6.10. Which contracts are "Project Contracts" therefore varies by provision and by an unmeasured efforts standard.

The Recitals define "Project Lenders" to include providers of supplier's credit as well as the Initial Lender and Subsequent Project Lenders, whereas the operative provisions (for example "Cash Sweep Debt Service" and "Lender") use the term as if it meant term loan lenders only. The recital definition and the operative use do not sit together.

Limbs (a) and (b) describe two overlapping periods — the fiscal year and a rolling half-year straddle — with no "or", "and" or rule for choosing between them. Which period a financial test is measured over is left open.

The date is "mutually determined by the Required Lenders and the Borrower at the time of Financial Closure" — an agreement to agree — subject only to a long-stop of 30 June 2013. Nothing says what the date is if the parties never agree.

The date can only be fixed "at the time of Financial Closure", yet Financial Closure under its own definition may never occur, while the First Sweep Period and the Force Majeure Event definition both run off the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date. Those provisions cannot operate if the triggering event does not happen.

The definition promises a "first perfected security interest in the Collateral ... including all assets and properties of the Borrower" but then subordinates the interest in Current Assets to a future Working Capital Bank lender. Whether the security is first-ranking depends on which half of the sentence prevails and on the vague "Current Assets" boundary.

The FACR definition assumes fixed assets "over which the Secured Parties have a first priority security interest (subject only to Permitted Liens)", which does not accommodate the Current Assets subordination created here. The two definitions describe the security package differently.

A factual representation — "the Borrower has no Subsidiary" — is embedded inside a definition, so it is unclear whether it operates as a defined meaning or as a warranty capable of breach. Its stated scope ("for purposes of the representations and warranties ... on the date hereof and on the Effective Date") adds a further limit.

The definition caps Supplier Financing at US$183,000,000 in aggregate, while "Financial Closure" requires Supplier Financing made available of US$182,750,000 and the Recitals put total supplier's credit within a US$713,000,000 package. The figures are close but not aligned, and the availability requirement is not tied to the cap.

The period ends 30 September 2013, yet Section 2.06 permits Letters of Credit issued to 30 June 2013 to be drawn much later and Section 2.06(e) converts each LC Disbursement automatically into a Term Loan. A Term Loan cannot arise after the commitments have lapsed under Section 2.01, and the two provisions are not reconciled.

The definition allows the Total Commitment only to be increased by Accession Agreements, while Section 2.08(a) provides that on a partial termination of Unused Commitments "the Total Commitments shall be adjusted accordingly" downwards. The defined amount and the operative reduction mechanism do not match.

Limb (b) adds "Working Capital Bank Finance", a term that is not defined; the defined term is "Working Capital Bank Financing", which the Short-Term Debt and Long-Term Debt definitions expressly deduct. Whether working capital debt is included or excluded from Total Debt is left uncertain.

The definition is a single run-on sentence that defines the loans partly by the restrictions applying to them and ends "certain of which ... are excluded from certain definitions as used herein", identifying neither the loans nor the definitions. It cannot be applied without going outside its own words.

The closing condition "on the same terms as the required by the Loans" is grammatically incomplete, leaving the test for including limbs (ii) and (iii) in the denominator unusable as written. The creditor's prepayment share depends on it.

The "Indebtedness" definition refers at limb (i) to obligations under "any Working Capital Bank Facility", a term never defined, while this definition creates "Working Capital Bank Financing". The two labels for the same facility are used inconsistently across the definitions.

The section provides that undrawn Term Loan Commitments "lapse automatically" at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period and that no re-borrowing is permitted, yet Section 2.06(e) makes every later LC Disbursement convert automatically into a Term Loan. Letters of Credit may run well past that date under Section 2.06(c), and the two provisions cannot both operate.

Tranche B becomes available only "on and after the Business Day on which Financial Closure shall occur", a condition whose satisfaction the Borrower cannot compel and which the section leaves entirely unallocated. Whether that is a true condition precedent to the Initial Lender's own US$100,000,000 commitment is squarely arguable.

Financial Closure requires Total Commitments of US$530,000,000, which under the "Total Commitment" and Section 2.20 definitions can only arise if third-party Subsequent Project Lenders choose to accede, while the Recitals state the lenders "shall provide" that sum. The availability of a committed tranche is thus made to depend on an event the operative provisions leave optional.

Borrowings "need not be ratable" among Lenders, yet Section 2.09 requires repayment "for the ratable account of the Lenders" and the pro rata definitions allocate prepayments by each Lender's share. How unratable drawings are repaid ratably is not addressed.

Every Borrowing must be a Eurodollar Rate Borrowing, but Section 2.04 provides that if a Eurodollar Rate Borrowing is unavailable the Lenders "shall have no obligation" to fund at any other rate. Read together, the funding obligation disappears whenever the required rate basis is unavailable.

"[I]n not more than fifteen (15) Borrowings" is grafted onto a minimum-amount sentence without saying over what period or facility the cap of fifteen operates. Whether it limits the Borrower's total draw-downs across the whole availability period is arguable.

The section says that if a Eurodollar Rate Borrowing is unavailable the Lenders "may" fund but "shall have no obligation to do so", and any alternative funding is in "their complete discretion". That is difficult to square with Section 2.01 and Section 2.02, which make the Total Commitment available to the Borrower on satisfaction of the Article IV conditions.

The availability cap is expressed through a chain of qualifications — the Unused Commitment of the Lender obliged to reimburse, "as reduced by any Borrowings under Section 2.02(a) or (b)", plus a proviso for undrawn expired Letters of Credit. What amount is actually available at any time is not readily determinable from the words.

The five specific documentary requirements are followed by "(vi) such other documents as may be specified by the Issuing Bank from time to time", an open catch-all that could swallow the enumerated list. Whether the Issuing Bank's discretion is bounded by the character of items (i)–(v) is the ejusdem generis question.

This limits expiry to the earlier of 36 months from issuance or four years from the date of the Agreement (29 December 2014), while the "Letter of Credit" definition allows negotiation until 30 December 2014. The two provisions fix inconsistent outer dates.

Automatic conversion of an LC Disbursement into a Term Loan can occur long after 30 September 2013, but Section 2.01 makes undrawn Term Loan Commitments lapse automatically at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period and Section 2.08(a) terminates them on the same day. The conversion mechanism has no commitment left to draw on.

The proviso preserves the Issuing Bank's liability for direct damages caused by its "failure to exercise care", and the next sentence then deems care to have been exercised in the absence of gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. The two sentences set different liability standards for the same conduct.

The statement that the Issuing Bank "will have the final word" and that the Borrower "will not question its decision" absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud sits against Section 2.06(f), which preserves the Borrower's claim for direct damages caused by a mere failure to exercise care. The two paragraphs give the Borrower different rights over the same determination.

"[P]ayable immediately on demand by the Borrower" reverses the parties: on its face the Borrower makes the demand for interest that is expressed to be for the Issuing Bank's account. The misplaced prepositional phrase changes who must act.

The enumeration reads "(i) ... and (iii)" with no clause (ii), so a step in the mechanism for setting Interest Periods on subsequent Borrowings is missing. The same defect appears in the "Interest Period" definition.

The election is to be made "in its first Borrowing Request", consistent with the "one-time request" definition of Interest Election Request, but Section 2.07 is drafted as a continuing power of "Interest Elections". Whether the Borrower retains any later election is not resolved.

The cancellation right is given "for any reason, including the deterioration in the Borrower's creditworthiness due to" three enumerated events, leaving a general catch-all sitting directly against specific examples. Whether the right is genuinely unlimited or confined to creditworthiness-type causes is the classic ejusdem generis dispute, and the one-sidedness invites construction against the drafter.

The same paragraph requires cancellation "upon prior written notice to the Borrower" yet permits it "immediately upon such notice", and then says that except for creditworthiness cases the Lender "shall endeavor to provide prior notice". Prior notice is thus mandatory and merely aspirational in the same sentence sequence.

An unfettered right to cancel Unused Commitments at any time is hard to reconcile with Section 2.01, which makes the Total Commitment available throughout the Term Loan Availability Period, and with Section 2.02(a)–(b), under which stated amounts "shall be available" once the Article IV conditions are met. Section 2.08(b), by contrast, bars the Borrower from reducing commitments at all before Financial Closure.

The Borrower's right to reduce commitments arises only "if the Project costs shall have been reduced below one billion ninety seven million Dollars", with no definition of Project costs and no mechanism for determining or evidencing the reduction. The condition cannot be tested on the words alone.

The proviso that a payment falling on a non-Business Day "shall be made on the next preceding Business Day" moves payments earlier, the reverse of the extension convention used in the "Interest Period" definition. The two conventions in one instrument produce different due dates.

The schedule amortises "all Term Loans outstanding on the last day of the Term Loan Availability Period", making no provision for Term Loans arising later by automatic conversion of LC Disbursements under Section 2.06(e). Those loans would have no repayment date short of the Term Loan Maturity Date.
